## The idea

Rhythm can be represented before a melody has any pitches. A sequence of durations already tells you where attacks occur, how long the pattern lasts, and which spans feel long or short in relation to the beat. Sonic Pi makes this representation direct because `sleep` accepts fractional beat values.

The historical names need one clear convention. In the system used throughout this book, a *quarter note* lasts 1 beat, an eighth note lasts `0.5`, and a sixteenth note lasts `0.25`. The fractions describe divisions of the quarter-note beat rather than fractions of a minute or second.

The renderer below accepts a duration array and a percussion sample. Since every attack has the same colour, the changing gaps carry the pattern. Clap along and keep the whole beat moving underneath the smaller values. If your clap loses its place, identify whether the half-beat or quarter-beat subdivision caused the break.

## Run this

```{.ruby audio=""}
use_bpm 96

durations = [1, 0.5, 0.5, 0.25, 0.25, 0.5, 1]

define :play_rhythm do |lengths, sound|
  lengths.each do |duration|
    sample sound, amp: 0.9, finish: [duration * 0.35, 1].min
    sleep duration
  end
end

puts "#{durations.sum} beats"
play_rhythm durations, :drum_tom_mid_soft
```

One drum colour marks seven attacks. The first occupies a full beat; two half-beat gaps divide the next beat; the two quarter-beat values compress the centre before another half beat and a final full beat. The printed sum gives the complete span. Because pitch, sample, and amplitude remain fixed, changes in density come from the duration array.

## Change one thing

1. Replace every `0.5` with `0.25`. More attacks now fit into less musical time, so the phrase shortens and its centre becomes denser. Count the new total before running it.

2. Restore the durations and change only the sample. Choose one with a longer tail and compare how clearly you can locate the same seven onsets. The score remains fixed even if articulation blurs its surface.

3. Return to the original sample. The program already prints `durations.sum`; alter one duration and predict the new result before pressing Run. Confirm that the printed total and the final onset pattern move together.

## Why it works

Durations form a timeline through addition. Their sum gives the phrase length. The sum of all values before a particular event gives that event's onset, often called a prefix sum in programming. For the array `[1, 0.5, 0.5]`, the attacks occur at beats 0, 1, and 1.5, and the complete span is 2 beats.

Those relationships explain the familiar subdivisions. Two eighth-note values of `0.5` occupy the same beat as one quarter-note value of `1`; four sixteenth-note values of `0.25` do the same. When clapping becomes uncertain, count the smallest subdivision long enough to place the attacks, then hear those smaller units inside the larger beat rather than allowing them to replace it.

The array is easy to validate and transform before playback. You can reject a bar with the wrong sum, double every value to augment the rhythm, or calculate all onset positions. The renderer does not need to know why a value is present. It advances by the supplied duration.

This small format carries a limitation. Each value acts both as the time until the next onset and, indirectly through `finish`, as part of the sounding articulation. It cannot describe two notes that overlap while a third begins in the gap. Later event scores will separate `:start` from `:duration` for that reason. Here, sequential prefix sums are enough and keep the arithmetic audible.

Sample length is not rhythmic duration. `finish` chooses how much of the recorded sample plays, while `sleep duration` schedules the following onset. A short source may end before a one-beat value has elapsed; a long tail may continue toward the next attack. Listen to the attack positions when checking rhythm and treat the tail as articulation, as you did with release in Lesson 7.

Lesson 13 uses equal subdivisions and adds recurring accents. The duration sum will establish the bar's extent, while the accents tell the ear how that span is grouped.

## Take it further

Write a rhythm interpreter that accepts a duration array and a sample symbol. Construct two patterns from quarter-, eighth-, and sixteenth-note values, with each pattern adding up to four beats. Print the sum before playback and reject any other total.

Add a quiet click on every whole beat in a separate thread, then clap each pattern against it. The same renderer should accept at least two sample symbols without changing its loop. During Sonic Pi 5 playback, note the first fractional value at which your clap drifts from the click. That observation tells you which subdivision needs to be counted more explicitly.
